It is worth noting that the wall thickness of the compressor has been carefully evaluated, and after the corrosion allowance is added, the resulting thickness comes to 63 mm. This value represents the culmination of a comprehensive assessment, ensuring that the casing is robust enough to withstand the operating conditions while also accounting for material loss over the service life. Furthermore, the 63 mm figure is not merely a number; it reflects a balanced consideration of safety, durability, and practicality, highlighting the importance of a meticulous design process.

In addition to the casing itself, attention must also be given to the gasket selection for the flanged joints, which plays a crucial role in overall performance. Two gasket materials are currently under consideration, and the comparison between them is based solely on temperature limit. While other factors such as cost and chemical compatibility are undoubtedly important, the temperature criterion serves as the decisive factor in this particular evaluation, underscoring the need to prioritise thermal performance above all else.

On this basis, the higher-rated material emerges as the preferred option. It offers a greater margin at elevated temperatures, ensuring reliable sealing performance even under demanding conditions, and thereby reducing the risk of leakage. The lower-rated alternative, by contrast, may be adequate under normal circumstances, but it provides less headroom when temperatures rise, which could potentially compromise the joint over time.

This approach is consistent with the treatment applied elsewhere in the unit, including the $\Delta P$ provisions for the absorber circuit and the NPSH considerations for the lean solvent pump, both of which were approached with a similar emphasis on conservative margins. Nevertheless, an important question remains regarding whether the higher-rated gasket material can be seated satisfactorily on the flange faces as specified, and this aspect will need to be examined further as the evaluation continues to develop and the remaining details are progressively addressed in due course as part of the ongoing assessment of the joint design as a whole

The compressor casing thickness stands at 63 mm once the corrosion allowance is added to the pressure-retaining thickness. That figure closes the casing calculation: the pressure term and the allowance enter separately, and the 63 mm value is the sum the fabricator works to, with no further margin layered on top. The margin question belongs to the pressure term, which was fixed with the design pressure for the absorber circuit, and the allowance follows the corrosion basis set for the gas side. Neither input is reopened here.

Attention turns to the flanged joints, where the gasket choice remains open between the two candidate materials. The comparison is made on temperature limit only. Pressure rating, chemical resistance and cost are excluded from this comparison, not because they are settled, but because the temperature limit is the property on which the two materials differ in a way that binds the design: the hotter joints sit downstream of the compressor discharge, and the gasket at those joints sees the highest metal temperature in the circuit.

On that single criterion the higher-rated material is preferred. The lower-rated material remains within its limit at the normal operating temperature, and its exclusion rests on the excursion case, where discharge temperature rises while the trip response is still developing. A gasket that is adequate at the normal point and marginal in the excursion leaves the joint dependent on the speed of a protective response; the higher-rated material removes that dependence.

The same discipline has governed the adjoining calculations. The $\Delta P$ allowance for the absorber circuit and the NPSH margin at the lean solvent pump were each fixed against the excursion case rather than the normal point, and the gasket choice is consistent with that treatment.
